analysis.one_liner: Raises estate and gift taxes on the largest fortunes and closes trust loopholes used to avoid them.
analysis.headline: The estate tax increase, backed by 34 House Democrats, never received a committee vote or floor action and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would raise estate and gift tax rates, with a 65% rate on estates over $1 billion, and cut the amount heirs can inherit tax-free from roughly $13 million to $3.5 million. It would close a set of trusts-and-valuation tricks — short-term trusts, grantor trusts, discounted interests in family businesses — that let very large fortunes pass with little or no estate tax. It also raises the special protections for family farms and donated conservation land so smaller landowners are not caught. Only about the top 0.5% of estates would owe more tax.
analysis.who_benefits: Nearly everyone except the wealthiest families. Because only about one-half of one percent of estates exceed the new $3.5 million threshold, almost no ordinary family would pay more; instead the added revenue would come from very large fortunes, easing the pressure to raise taxes elsewhere or borrow. Families donating conservation land and some farm owners get larger special exclusions. The bill's title reflects that it targets the top 0.5%.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Everyone except the wealthiest 0.5% of estates

how_it_helps.text: Only estates over $3.5 million would pay estate tax, leaving about 99.5% of estates untouched while very large fortunes pay more.
Estates over $1 billion would face a 65% rate, and estates over $10 million a 50% rate, up from the current 40% top rate.

The bill closes avoidance tools: it would no longer allow valuation discounts for family-controlled businesses, would require grantor retained annuity trusts to last at least 10 years and retain at least 25% of the trust's value, and would pull grantor trust assets back into the taxable estate at death.
The estate tax exclusion for donated conservation easements rises from $500,000 to $2 million and the covered share from 40% to 60%, rewarding families who protect land.
The special farm real-property exclusion rises from $750,000 to $3 million, indexed for inflation, shielding family farms from valuation-driven estate taxes.

analysis.who_pays: Heirs to estates worth more than $3.5 million, especially billionaires facing the new 65% rate, and the wealth-management industry that sells estate-tax avoidance structures. Certain aggressive gift-trust arrangements would also face new tax, and the annual gift exclusion for hard-to-value transfers drops to $10,000 per recipient.

drawbacks.text: The bill slashes the lifetime estate and gift exclusion from roughly $13 million to $3.5 million and drops the top rate to 65%, which would make estate planning substantially more complicated and expensive even for moderately wealthy families.

The ban on any valuation discount for family-controlled entities and on discounts for passive assets inside holding companies could hit legitimate family businesses, not just tax avoidance, if those holdings are not clearly used in an active trade or business.

The simplified annual gift exclusion drops to $10,000 per recipient and adds an aggregate per-donor cap for trust and hard-to-liquidate transfers, a reduction from the current annual exclusion that could affect donors beyond the ultra-wealthy.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains concentrate on the public budget and fairness side: substantial new revenue from a group — sub-billion-dollar families are largely spared, billion-dollar estates are not — that currently shields enormous sums through trust and valuation devices. The main honest cost is complexity: estate planning rules would change significantly and some family-business transfers could face valuation disputes. The farm and conservation carve-outs address the most common objection that family farms and protected land would be hit.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a markup, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jimmy Gomez introduced the For the 99.5 Percent Act on April 18, 2023.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which was its last recorded action.
No further action — no subcommittee or full committee markup, no committee vote, no floor debate — appears in the bill's history through the end of the 118th Congress in January 2025.
The bill had 33 cosponsors, all Democrats, in addition to its Democratic sponsor.
The bill would raise estate tax rates up to 65% for estates over $1 billion and cut the basic exclusion amount to $3.5 million.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The roughly 0.5% of estates large enough to face the new taxes — and the trust and estate-planning industry that serves them — are better off because the bill never advanced: no higher rates, no loophole closures, and the larger pre-existing exclusion stayed in place for 2024 and 2025.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Billionaire estates and their estate planners

industries.note: Estates over $3.5 million would owe more, with a 65% rate above $1 billion, and grantor trust and family-business discount techniques would no longer erase taxable value. Estate-tax avoidance shifts the tax burden onto everyone else, so the industry's interest runs against the public's.

industries.industry: Trust and estate planning industry (wealth advisors and estate attorneys)
